title: MC2 Data description
text:
This folder contains the data for the anomalous postings originating from Tenant Thread.
This data is based on the actions taken by the employees and personal agents inside of Tenant Thread.


The anomalous posting is sent to SaidIt by John Windward on May 17, 2046 at 4:21am.



MC2_Data.json – A timeline of events gathered by the internal systems. org_chart.json – The organization chart of Tenant Thread including people and departments. Compatible with networkX node_link_graph.

The data is structured as a timeline. The events are ordered and indicate the operations performed by people, autonomous agents and office systems.

The contents vary by the contents of short_name. - id: A unique id for each record.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
This report applies visual analytics to a real-world motor insurance portfolio from a Spanish non-life insurer. The exercise brief asks for R-based visual analytics that go beyond dashboard reporting and help discover factors linked to portfolio profitability and volatility.
The report is organised in the following structure: context first, analytical sandbox, data preparation, univariate exploration, bivariate analysis, statistical validation, and final findings. The analysis uses the Mendeley motor portfolio data.
Two analytical definitions are used throughout the report:

Profitability is measured by aggregate profit = total_premium - total_incurred and by aggregate loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium. Lower loss ratio indicates better underwriting profitability before expenses.
Volatility is measured by claim occurrence, claim frequency, capped individual loss ratio, high-loss policy rate, and upper-tail loss-ratio behaviour.

The main question is: which portfolio segments show weaker profitability or higher volatility, and are those patterns visually and statistically defensible?

4 Task 2: Bivariate visual analytics and validation
Bivariate analysis compares profitability and volatility across time and major risk-related segments. It builds on the Section 3 finding that the portfolio is zero-inflated at policy level but exposed to a small positive-loss tail, especially through liability_incurred and other incurred-cost components. The comparisons use the data dictionary meaning of each segment: coverage structure, claims-history quality, billing frequency, fuel type, circulation area, driver/vehicle characteristics, and exposure-adjusted claim outcomes.

Observations

The year-level table uses year as the calendar-year policy period and provides the numeric baseline for exposure, premium, incurred loss, profit, claim frequency, and loss ratio.
Aggregate loss ratio rises from 65.6% in 2022 to 66.5% in 2023 and 74.7% in 2024, showing a clear deterioration in underwriting profitability.
Claim frequency also rises slightly from 0.302 to 0.312, while the high-loss policy share increases from 8.0% to 9.7%.
This pattern links the Section 3 positive-loss tail to a time trend: 2024 is not only larger in exposure, but also more loss-heavy.




Show the code
trend_amount_df <- yearly |>
  select(year, Premium = premium, Incurred = incurred, Profit = profit) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "measure", values_to = "amount") |>
  mutate(hover = paste0(
    "Year: ", year,
    "<br>Measure: ", measure,
    "<br>Amount: ", money(amount)
  ))

trend_amount <- trend_amount_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = amount, colour = measure, group = measure, text = hover)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = money) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium, incurred loss, and profit by year",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Aggregate amount"
  )

trend_lr_df <- yearly |>
  mutate(hover = paste0(
    "Year: ", year,
    "<br>Loss ratio: ", pct(loss_ratio)
  ))

trend_lr <- trend_lr_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = loss_ratio, group = 1, text = hover)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  labs(
    title = "Aggregate loss ratio by year",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Loss ratio"
  )

subplot(
  ggplotly(trend_amount, tooltip = "text"),
  ggplotly(trend_lr, tooltip = "text"),
  widths = c(0.58, 0.42),
  margin = 0.06,
  titleX = TRUE,
  titleY = TRUE
) |>
  layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.2))







Observations

Premium and incurred losses both increase over time, but incurred losses grow faster in 2024.
Aggregate profit remains positive, so the issue is not absolute loss-making at portfolio level; the issue is a weaker margin.
The right-hand loss-ratio panel makes the deterioration easier to see than the amount plot alone because it standardises incurred loss against premium.
The visual signal supports treating 2024 as an early-warning period for deeper segment checks.

The policy-type table ranks coverage structures by aggregate loss ratio and separates product profitability from individual policy-year spread.
COMP_N means comprehensive without excess and has the weakest aggregate result with a 93.9% loss ratio; COMP_E means comprehensive with excess and follows at 73.8%.
COMP_N also has the highest claim frequency at about 1.046 claims per exposure unit and the highest high-loss policy share at 20.8%, consistent with broader first-party coverage exposure.
This aligns with Section 3’s incurred-cost observation: profitability pressure is driven by claim occurrence and tail losses rather than by premium distribution alone.




Show the code
overall_loss_ratio <- sum(motor$total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(motor$total_premium, na.rm = TRUE)

policy_lr <- policy_tbl |>

    policy_type = fct_reorder(policy_type, loss_ratio),
    label = paste0(pct(loss_ratio), " | exp ", comma(round(exposure)))

  geom_vline(xintercept = overall_loss_ratio, linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#08519c") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8, colour = "red") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = overall_loss_ratio, xend = loss_ratio, yend = policy_type), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(size = exposure), colour = "#08519c", alpha = 0.82) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.08, size = 3.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = pct,

  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma, range = c(3, 8)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Aggregate loss ratio by policy type",
    subtitle = "Blue line marks the overall portfolio loss ratio; red dashed line marks 100% break-even before expenses.",
    x = "Aggregate loss ratio",
    y = NULL,
    size = "Exposure"

  theme(plot.margin = margin(5.5, 35, 5.5, 5.5))

policy_box <- motor |>
  filter(!is.na(policy_type), !is.na(loss_ratio_cap)) |>

COMP_N and COMP_E are the main policy-type segments requiring closer monitoring because they represent comprehensive cover, with and without excess respectively.
Most policy-year records still have zero or low individual loss ratios, so the boxplot does not suggest that every comprehensive-cover policy performs poorly.
Weak segment performance is concentrated in claim frequency and upper-tail loss outcomes, consistent with the zero-inflated distributions observed in Section 3.
The dot plot compares each policy type with the overall portfolio loss ratio and the 100% break-even line, while the labels show both percentage loss ratio and total exposure.




4.3 Segment scan: bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area


Show the code
overall_loss_ratio <- sum(motor$total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(motor$total_premium, na.rm = TRUE)

seg_long <- bind_rows(
  portfolio_summary(motor, bonus_score) |>
    mutate(segment = "Bonus score", category = as.character(bonus_score)),
  portfolio_summary(motor, fuel_type) |>
    mutate(segment = "Fuel type", category = fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(fuel_type), "Missing") |> as.character()),
  portfolio_summary(motor, circulation_area) |>
    mutate(segment = "Circulation area", category = as.character(circulation_area)),
  portfolio_summary(motor, payment_frequency) |>
    mutate(segment = "Payment frequency", category = as.character(payment_frequency))
)

seg_long |>
  mutate(
    category = fct_reorder(category, loss_ratio),
    label = paste0(pct(loss_ratio), " | exp ", comma(round(exposure)))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio, y = category)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = overall_loss_ratio, linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#08519c") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8, colour = "red") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = overall_loss_ratio, xend = loss_ratio, yend = category), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(size = exposure, colour = segment), alpha = 0.82, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 2.7, show.legend = FALSE) +

    title = "Loss ratio differs across risk-related categories",
    subtitle = "Blue line marks the overall portfolio loss ratio; red dashed line marks 100% break-even before expenses.",

    size = "Exposure"

  theme(plot.margin = margin(5.5, 55, 5.5, 5.5))










Observations

Non-good bonus scores show weaker experience: neutral N and poor-history B have loss ratios of about 81.4% and 79.0%, compared with 69.7% for favourable-history G.
Diesel vehicles (D) have a higher loss ratio than gasoline vehicles (G), about 73.0% versus 64.3%.
Urban circulation areas (U) have a higher loss ratio than rural areas (R), about 71.4% versus 68.9%.
Semi-annual (S) and quarterly (Q) payment frequencies have higher loss ratios than annual (A) payment, so billing pattern is a useful screening variable.
The dot-plot labels add total exposure, making it easier to separate materially important categories from small or sparse categories.
These visual signals are not causal by themselves because exposure, product mix, vehicle profile, and policy type can differ across segments.




4.4 Policy type by year heatmap


Show the code

  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = pct(loss_ratio)), colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#2c7fb8", high = "#d7301f", labels = pct) +

    subtitle = "Darker red cells identify combinations needing closer monitoring.",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Loss ratio"
  )










Observations

The heatmap links the year-level deterioration with policy-type differences.
COMP_N, comprehensive without excess, is the clearest 2024 hotspot, with a loss ratio slightly above break-even at about 102.4%.
COMP_N worsens from 72.8% in 2022 to 92.3% in 2023 and 102.4% in 2024, suggesting persistent deterioration rather than a one-year isolated cell.
COMP_E, comprehensive with excess, also rises in 2024, reinforcing that comprehensive-cover segments should be monitored separately from third-party-focused covers such as TP and TPG.




4.5 Brand-level volatility screen


Show the code
brand_tbl <- motor |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    high_loss_rate = mean(loss_ratio > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(exposure >= 1000) |>
  mutate(hover = paste0(
    "Brand: ", vehicle_brand,
    "<br>Exposure: ", comma(exposure),
    "<br>Claim frequency: ", number(claim_frequency, accuracy = 0.01),
    "<br>Loss ratio: ", pct(loss_ratio),
    "<br>Premium: ", money(premium),
    "<br>Incurred: ", money(incurred),
    "<br>Claims: ", comma(claims)
  ))

brand_volatility_plot <- brand_tbl |>
  ggplot(aes(x = claim_frequency, y = loss_ratio, size = exposure, text = hover)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, colour = "#08519c") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = brand_tbl |> slice_max(loss_ratio, n = 8),
    aes(label = vehicle_brand),
    size = 3,
    max.overlaps = 20
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma, range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(
    title = "Brand-level screen for high loss ratio and claim frequency",
    subtitle = "Only brands with exposure >= 1,000 are shown.",
    x = "Claim frequency",
    y = "Aggregate loss ratio",
    size = "Exposure"
  )

ggplotly(brand_volatility_plot, tooltip = "text")







Observations

The bubble chart screens brands by claim frequency, loss ratio, and exposure.
Upper-right brands combine higher claim frequency and higher loss ratio, so they represent volatility candidates rather than automatically poor brands; brand can proxy vehicle profile, repair cost, parts availability, and theft attractiveness.
Among brands with exposure at least 1,000, Mitsubishi and Mazda have the highest aggregate loss ratios, about 99.8% and 93.9% respectively.
Large upper-right bubbles should be prioritised for deeper investigation because they combine underwriting impact with enough exposure to matter.




4.6 Statistical validation
The dataset is large and skewed, so visual signals are validated with non-parametric and categorical tests:

Kruskal-Wallis tests check whether capped individual loss ratio differs across segment groups.
Chi-square tests check whether claim occurrence differs across segment groups.
Spearman correlations check monotonic relationships between numerical variables and capped loss ratio.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
5 Key findings
The objective of this report is to use visual analytics to identify portfolio segments associated with weaker underwriting profitability and higher volatility. The main findings are:

The portfolio is profitable overall, but the margin is exposed to loss volatility. Across 354,140 policy-year records, the portfolio generates about EUR31.2 million underwriting profit before expenses and an aggregate loss ratio of about 70.3%. However, only about 14.3% of records have claims, so profitability is sensitive to a relatively small claim-producing tail.
Profitability deteriorates in 2024. The aggregate loss ratio increases from about 65.6% in 2022 and 66.5% in 2023 to about 74.7% in 2024. This indicates that incurred losses are growing faster than premium and that the latest year should be treated as an early-warning period.
Policy type is the strongest and most defensible segmentation signal. Comprehensive covers have materially weaker results than third-party-focused covers. COMP_N has the highest aggregate loss ratio at about 93.9%, and the year-by-policy heatmap shows COMP_N exceeding break-even in 2024 at about 102.4%.
Secondary segment variables explain where profitability and volatility are concentrated. Non-good bonus scores, diesel vehicles, urban circulation areas, and shorter payment frequencies show higher loss ratios than their comparison groups. These are useful underwriting screening variables, but they should be interpreted together with exposure and policy mix.
Volatility is concentrated in claim frequency and upper-tail outcomes rather than in the typical policy-year record. Boxplots, capped loss-ratio distributions, policy-type comparisons, and brand-level bubbles show that most records remain low-loss, while a smaller set of claim-heavy segments drives the high-loss tail.
The visual signals are statistically supported but not causal. Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests support group differences across key segmentation variables. Because the dataset is large and observational, the results should guide deeper underwriting investigation rather than be used as standalone pricing rules.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
6 Recommendations

Prioritise comprehensive-cover review. Monitor COMP_N and COMP_E separately from the rest of the portfolio, with particular attention to 2024 COMP_N performance. Review claim frequency, claim severity, excess structure, and premium adequacy before making portfolio-wide pricing changes.
Use 2024 as an early-warning trigger. Build a recurring year-by-segment loss-ratio monitor so that deterioration by policy type, bonus score, fuel type, circulation area, and payment frequency is detected before it becomes an aggregate profitability issue.
Apply segment screening, not automatic repricing. Treat high-loss brand, diesel, urban, non-good bonus-score, and shorter-payment-frequency groups as candidates for deeper review. Validate whether the observed differences remain after controlling for exposure, policy type, vehicle age, driver age, and claim mix.
Strengthen volatility management. Track high-loss policy rate, claim frequency, severity, and capped loss ratio in addition to aggregate loss ratio. These measures align better with the report objective because they reveal tail-risk segments hidden by portfolio-level profitability.
Enrich the portfolio data before final underwriting action. Add external geography, traffic-density, weather, theft-risk, and vehicle repair-cost indicators to explain why specific segments underperform and to separate true risk effects from product-mix effects.

Part 1: Network data with tidygraph, ggraph, and visNetwork
This section uses the GAStech email data. The nodes file contains employee information, while the edges file contains email communication records.

1.1 Load R packages

pacman::p_load(
  igraph, tidygraph, ggraph,
  visNetwork, lubridate, clock,
  tidyverse, graphlayouts,
  concaveman, ggforce
)

The main packages are:

tidygraph for creating and manipulating graph objects.
ggraph for static network visualisation.
visNetwork for interactive network visualisation.
lubridate for handling dates.



1.2 Import network data

network_data_dir <- "../data/r4va/chap27"

GAStech_nodes <- read_csv(file.path(network_data_dir, "GAStech_email_node.csv"))
GAStech_edges <- read_csv(file.path(network_data_dir, "GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv"))

The nodes table describes the employees. The edges table records who sent email to whom, together with the date, time, subject, and email labels.

The first check is to inspect the data structure. In the raw data, SentDate is usually imported as character, so it must be converted before weekday analysis.


1.3 Prepare date and weekday fields

GAStech_edges <- GAStech_edges %>%
  mutate(SendDate = dmy(SentDate)) %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(
    SentDate,
    label = TRUE,
    abbr = FALSE
  ))

dmy() converts the date string into a proper date. wday() extracts the weekday so that email patterns can be compared across days.


1.4 Aggregate email links

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
  summarise(Weight = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(source != target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1)

The raw edge data contains one row per email. For network visualisation, the emails are aggregated by sender, receiver, and weekday. Weight shows how many emails were sent for each relationship.


1.5 Create a tidygraph object

GAStech_graph <- tbl_graph(
  nodes = GAStech_nodes,
  edges = GAStech_edges_aggregated,
  directed = TRUE
)

A tbl_graph stores the node table and edge table together. Since email has a sender and receiver, the graph is directed.

Sorting the edges by Weight helps identify stronger communication links.


1.6 Basic static network graph

ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()








This first graph shows the basic network structure. The layout is simple and is mainly used to check whether the graph has been created correctly.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()








theme_graph() removes unnecessary chart elements and gives the network plot a cleaner appearance.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = "grey50")) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = "grey40"))

g + theme_graph(
  background = "grey10",
  text_colour = "white"
)








The colour and background can be adjusted to improve contrast.


1.7 Improve layout and visual encoding

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()








The Fruchterman-Reingold layout places connected nodes closer together.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes(
    colour = Department,
    size = 3

g + theme_graph()








Colouring nodes by department makes it easier to see whether communication is concentrated within or across departments.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 3
  )

g + theme_graph()








Edge width is mapped to email frequency. Thicker edges represent stronger communication links.


1.8 Facet network graphs

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 2
  )

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)








Faceting by weekday allows daily communication patterns to be compared.

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 2
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)








Moving the legend to the bottom makes the small multiples easier to read.

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 2
  )

g + facet_edges(~Weekday) +
  th_foreground(
    foreground = "grey80",
    border = TRUE
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








The foreground panel border makes each weekday panel clearer.

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = Department),
    size = 2
  )

g + facet_nodes(~Department) +
  th_foreground(
    foreground = "grey80",
    border = TRUE
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Faceting by department separates the employees into groups and helps identify department-level communication patterns.


1.9 Add network measures

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(
    colour = Department,
    size = betweenness_centrality
  ))

g + theme_graph()








Betweenness centrality highlights employees who sit between other employees in the communication network. Larger nodes are more important connectors.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(
    colour = Department,
    size = centrality_betweenness()
  ))

g + theme_graph()








The same measure can also be calculated directly inside the plot aesthetic.


1.10 Detect communities

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight,
      directed = TRUE
    )
  )) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community))

g + theme_graph()








Community detection groups employees who are more closely connected to each other.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(
    community = as.factor(group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
    betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()
  ) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(
      x, y,
      group = community,
      fill = community
    ),
    alpha = 0.2,
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")
  ) +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(
      fill = Department,
      size = betweenness_measure
    ),
    color = "black",
    shape = 21
  )

g + theme_graph()








The hulls show the detected communities. Node size still represents betweenness centrality.


1.11 Create an interactive network
visNetwork uses different edge column names. The edge table is rebuilt with from, to, and weight.

GAStech_edges_vis <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
  summarise(weight = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(from != to) %>%
  filter(weight > 1)


visNetwork(GAStech_nodes, GAStech_edges_vis)





This creates a basic interactive graph.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes, GAStech_edges_vis) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr")





The layout can be improved by using an igraph layout algorithm.

GAStech_nodes_vis <- GAStech_nodes %>%
  rename(group = Department)

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes_vis, GAStech_edges_vis) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)





The group column controls node colour, and the legend explains the department colours.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes_vis, GAStech_edges_vis) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visEdges(
    arrows = "to",
    smooth = list(
      enabled = TRUE,
      type = "curvedCW"
    )
  ) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)





Arrows show the direction of emails.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes_vis, GAStech_edges_vis) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = TRUE,
    nodesIdSelection = TRUE
  ) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)





highlightNearest and nodesIdSelection make the graph easier to explore interactively.

Part 2: Text data with tidytext
This section uses text documents from the 20 Newsgroups dataset. The workflow imports many text files, cleans the text, tokenises words, calculates TF-IDF, and builds a bigram network.

2.1 Load R packages

pacman::p_load(
  tidytext, widyr, wordcloud, DT, ggwordcloud,
  textplot, lubridate, hms, tidyverse,
  tidygraph, ggraph, igraph
)

package 'tokenizers' successfully unpacked and MD5 sums checked

package 'textplot' successfully unpacked and MD5 sums checked

The downloaded binary packages are in
    C:\Users\19154\AppData\Local\Temp\Rtmp4aRNo4\downloaded_packages




2.2 Import many text files

news20 <- "../data/r4va/chap29/20news/"

The folder should contain one subfolder per newsgroup. Each subfolder contains individual text files.

read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder, full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file, read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(
      id = basename(file),
      text
    ) %>%
    unnest(text)
}

This helper function reads all files in one folder and returns a tidy data frame.

raw_text <- tibble(folder = dir(news20, full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder, read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(
    newsgroup = basename(folder),
    id,
    text
  )

write_rds(raw_text, "../data/r4va/news20.rds")

The result has one row per line of text. The newsgroup column records which group the message belongs to.


2.3 Explore message counts

raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  summarise(messages = n_distinct(id), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(messages, newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of messages",
    y = NULL
  )








This bar chart checks whether the groups have similar or different numbers of messages.


2.4 Clean the text

cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(
    cumsum(text == "") > 0,
    cumsum(str_detect(text, "^--")) == 0
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

This step removes email headers and lines after automated signatures.

cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]") | text == "",
    !str_detect(text, "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
    !str_detect(text, "^In article <")
  )

This step removes quoted replies and other repeated email text.


2.5 Tokenise words

usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
    !word %in% stop_words$word
  )

unnest_tokens() splits text into one word per row. Stop words such as common articles and connectors are removed.

usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 61 × 2
   word          n
   <chr>     <int>
 1 game         12
 2 image        12
 3 mission      12
 4 orbit        12
 5 rendering    12
 6 satellite    12
 7 team         12
 8 baseball     10
 9 graphics     10
10 health       10
# ℹ 51 more rows


This count shows the most frequent remaining words.


2.6 Visualise words

words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()


wordcloud(
  words_by_newsgroup$word,
  words_by_newsgroup$n,
  max.words = 300
)








The word cloud gives a quick overview of frequent words.

set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    label = word,
    size = n
  )) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)








Faceting the word cloud by newsgroup makes group-level differences easier to compare.


2.7 Calculate TF-IDF

tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))

TF-IDF gives higher scores to words that are common in one newsgroup but less common in others.

DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = "top") %>%
  formatRound(
    columns = c("tf", "idf", "tf_idf"),
    digits = 3
  ) %>%
  formatStyle(
    0,
    target = "row",
    lineHeight = "25%"
  )





An interactive table is useful for searching and checking TF-IDF values.

tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    tf_idf,
    word,
    fill = newsgroup
  )) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~newsgroup,
    scales = "free"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "tf-idf",
    y = NULL
  )








This plot highlights the most distinctive terms in science-related newsgroups.


2.8 Correlate words across groups

newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  pairwise_cor(
    newsgroup,
    word,
    n,
    sort = TRUE
  )

Word correlation shows which newsgroups use similar vocabularies.

set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > 0.025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(
    alpha = correlation,
    width = correlation
  )) +
  geom_node_point(
    size = 6,
    color = "lightblue"
  ) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = name),
    color = "red",
    repel = TRUE
  ) +
  theme_void()








The graph connects newsgroups with similar word usage.


2.9 Work with bigrams

bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(
    bigram,
    text,
    token = "ngrams",
    n = 2
  )

bigrams

# A tibble: 336 × 3
   newsgroup     id      bigram          
   <chr>         <chr>   <chr>           
 1 comp.graphics 001.txt <NA>            
 2 comp.graphics 001.txt graphics image  
 3 comp.graphics 001.txt image rendering 
 4 comp.graphics 001.txt rendering pixel 
 5 comp.graphics 001.txt pixel color     
 6 comp.graphics 001.txt color software  
 7 comp.graphics 001.txt software display
 8 comp.graphics 001.txt display image   
 9 comp.graphics 001.txt image rendering 
10 comp.graphics 001.txt graphics image  
# ℹ 326 more rows


A bigram is a pair of consecutive words. Bigrams help show common phrases, not just single words.

bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != "NA") %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)

bigrams_count

# A tibble: 145 × 2
   bigram                 n
   <chr>              <int>
 1 team game              6
 2 disease hospital       4
 3 doctor patient         4
 4 graphics image         4
 5 image rendering        4
 6 league player          4
 7 league season          4
 8 medicine treatment     4
 9 patient health         4
10 satellite mission      4
# ℹ 135 more rows


This identifies the most common word pairs.

bigrams_separated <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != "NA") %>%
  separate(
    bigram,
    c("word1", "word2"),
    sep = " "
  )

bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word)

bigrams_filtered

# A tibble: 316 × 4
   newsgroup     id      word1     word2    
   <chr>         <chr>   <chr>     <chr>    
 1 comp.graphics 001.txt graphics  image    
 2 comp.graphics 001.txt image     rendering
 3 comp.graphics 001.txt rendering pixel    
 4 comp.graphics 001.txt pixel     color    
 5 comp.graphics 001.txt color     software 
 6 comp.graphics 001.txt software  display  
 7 comp.graphics 001.txt display   image    
 8 comp.graphics 001.txt image     rendering
 9 comp.graphics 001.txt graphics  image    
10 comp.graphics 001.txt image     rendering
# ℹ 306 more rows


The bigram is split into two columns so that stop words can be removed from both positions.


2.10 Build a bigram network

bigram_counts <- bigrams_filtered %>%
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE)


bigram_graph <- bigram_counts %>%
  filter(n > 3) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame()

bigram_graph

IGRAPH b302b84 DN-- 19 12 -- 
+ attr: name (v/c), n (e/n)
+ edges from b302b84 (vertex names):
 [1] team     ->game      disease  ->hospital  doctor   ->patient  
 [4] graphics ->image     image    ->rendering league   ->player   
 [7] league   ->season    medicine ->treatment patient  ->health   
[10] satellite->mission   science  ->mission   season   ->score    


The bigram graph treats words as nodes and common word pairs as directed edges.

set.seed(1234)

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point() +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = name),
    vjust = 1,
    hjust = 1
  )








This first network shows the basic bigram structure.

set.seed(1234)

a <- grid::arrow(
  type = "closed",
  length = unit(0.15, "inches")
)

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(edge_alpha = n),
    show.legend = FALSE,
    arrow = a,
    end_cap = circle(0.07, "inches")
  ) +
  geom_node_point(
    color = "lightblue",
    size = 5
  ) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = name),
    vjust = 1,
    hjust = 1
  ) +
  theme_void()








Arrows show word order, and edge transparency shows how frequently each bigram appears.

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
usr <- par("usr")
on.exit(par(usr))
par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")

text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

1.3.1 R Graphics VS ggplot
Base R gives a quick one-shot chart, while ggplot2 builds the chart in layers and gives more control.

hist(exam_data$MATHS)








Layman explanation: Line 1: hist(exam_data$MATHS) — Uses base R to draw a quick histogram of the Maths scores.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=10,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color="black",
                 fill="grey") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores")








Layman explanation: Line 1: ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) + — Starts a ggplot using the exam data and maps MATHS to the x-axis. The plus sign means another layer follows. Line 2: geom_histogram(bins=10, — This splits the Maths scores into 10 bins so the histogram has 10 groups. Line 3: boundary = 100, — This sets the bin boundary around 100 so the histogram starts at a sensible edge. Line 4: color="black", — This gives the bars a black outline. Line 5: fill="grey") + — This fills the bars with grey. The plus sign means another layer follows. Line 6: ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores") — Adds a title to the plot.

ggplot(data=exam_data,

Line 3: geom_boxplot() + — Summarises each group with a boxplot that shows the median, spread, and possible outliers. The plus sign means another layer follows. Line 5: fun = "mean", — This tells ggplot to calculate the mean as the summary value. Line 6: colour ="red", — This makes the summary point red so it stands out. Line 6: colour="red", — This makes the summary point red so it stands out. Line 7: size=4) — This makes the summary point larger so it is easier to notice.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Project objective
Main question: Which motor insurance portfolio segments show weaker profitability or higher volatility, and are those patterns visually and statistically defensible?

Profitability: profit = total_premium - total_incurred; loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium.
Volatility: claim occurrence, claim frequency, capped individual loss ratio, high-loss rate, and upper-tail behaviour.
Approach: combine univariate distribution checks, bivariate segment comparisons, and statistical validation.


This deck is aligned with the technical report objective. The goal is not only to describe the portfolio, but to identify where profitability and volatility risks are concentrated.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Finding 1: profitability weakened in 2024


Loss ratio rises from about 65.6% in 2022 to 74.7% in 2024.
This is an early-warning signal: incurred losses are growing faster than premium.


The key message is not that the portfolio is loss-making. It remains profitable before expenses, but the margin is weakening in 2024.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Finding 2: volatility is tail-driven


Most policy-year records have no claims.
A smaller positive-claim tail drives incurred loss and volatility.
This justifies using capped loss ratio, claim frequency, and high-loss indicators.


The univariate view supports the report’s focus on volatility: averages alone hide the small but material claim-producing tail.

Finding 3: policy type is the strongest signal


COMP_N has the highest aggregate loss ratio, about 93.9%.
COMP_E follows at about 73.8%, and both comprehensive covers need separate monitoring.
Most policy-year records remain low-loss; weak performance is concentrated in claim frequency and upper-tail outcomes.


The blue line is the overall portfolio loss ratio. The red dashed line is the 100% break-even line before expenses.

Finding 4: 2024 COMP_N is the clearest hotspot


COMP_N worsens across the period and reaches about 102.4% in 2024.
COMP_E also rises in 2024, reinforcing separate comprehensive-cover monitoring.


The heatmap makes the recommendation more specific: review comprehensive-cover performance, especially COMP_N in 2024.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Finding 5: secondary segment signals


Non-good bonus scores, diesel vehicles, urban circulation, and shorter payment frequencies show weaker experience.
These are screening variables, not standalone causal conclusions.


Exposure labels are important because segment materiality depends on both loss ratio and portfolio size.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Finding 6: brand-level volatility screen


Upper-right brands combine higher claim frequency and higher loss ratio.
Mitsubishi and Mazda have the highest aggregate loss ratios among brands with exposure at least 1,000.
Large upper-right bubbles should be prioritised because they combine impact with enough exposure to matter.


This is an exploratory screen. It supports deeper investigation rather than immediate brand-level pricing action.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Key findings

The portfolio is profitable overall, but the margin is exposed to a small claim-producing tail.
Profitability deteriorates in 2024: aggregate loss ratio rises from 65.6% to 74.7%.
Policy type is the strongest signal; COMP_N reaches 93.9% overall and 102.4% in 2024.
Bonus score, fuel type, circulation area, and payment frequency explain where weaker experience concentrates.
Volatility is concentrated in claim frequency and upper-tail outcomes, not the typical record.
Statistical tests support the visual signals, but the evidence remains observational and non-causal.


This slide condenses the report’s key findings and keeps them tied to the project objective: profitability and volatility discovery.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Recommendations

Prioritise comprehensive-cover review: monitor COMP_N and COMP_E, especially 2024 COMP_N, before broad pricing changes.
Use 2024 as an early-warning trigger: build year-by-segment loss-ratio monitoring across product and risk groups.
Apply segment screening, not automatic repricing: validate brand, diesel, urban, non-good bonus-score, and short-payment signals with controls.
Strengthen volatility management: track high-loss rate, claim frequency, severity, and capped loss ratio alongside aggregate loss ratio.
Enrich portfolio data before final underwriting action: add geography, traffic, weather, theft-risk, and repair-cost indicators.


The recommendations are practical next steps, not automatic repricing rules. They preserve the distinction between visual discovery and confirmatory underwriting analysis.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Closing message
Visual analytics identifies where the portfolio needs attention:

2024 deterioration is the main time-based warning.
Comprehensive cover is the main product-based warning.
Tail-risk metrics are needed because portfolio averages hide claim volatility.
The evidence should guide investigation and enrichment before pricing action.


The closing message links the report evidence back to the project objective and explains how visual analytics supports underwriting decision-making.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: VAST Mini-Challenge 1
text:
This report builds a visual analytics workflow for VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1. The case asks whether TenantThread’s inappropriate pre-embargo release of the CivicLoom merger was a deliberate leak or a system breakdown under crisis pressure.
The analysis uses the internal communications, public FleX posts, agent deliberations, and environmental context recorded in MC1_final_00.json.
The working conclusion is:






Important



The release was not an accidental one-message failure. The records show an intentional early-release sequence after SaltWind published the merger story at 5:00 PM. Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent reframed the 6:00 PM embargo as moot, claimed CivicLoom verbal consent, instructed PR-Intern to publish, and amplified the merger from personal and anonymous accounts before 6:00 PM. However, the system also broke down structurally: Judge warnings were exceeded, personal/anonymous channels were not controlled, and sentiment/market-survival logic displaced embargo enforcement.


Important evidence limitation: the dataset contains agent communications. It records Legal-Agent’s claim that CivicLoom verbal consent was obtained, but it does not independently verify that consent.

text:
2 Analytical sandbox


Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)

library(widyr)
library(ggwordcloud)
library(tidygraph)
library(ggraph)
library(plotly)
library(DT)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
set.seed(608)

`%||%` <- function(x, y) {
  if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) y else x
}

collapse_text <- function(x) {
  if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) return("")
  if (is.list(x)) x <- unlist(x, recursive = TRUE, use.names = FALSE)
  paste(as.character(x), collapse = " | ")
}

mc1_file <- if (file.exists("TH_Ex/data/th_ex2/raw/MC1_final_00.json")) {
  "TH_Ex/data/th_ex2/raw/MC1_final_00.json"
} else {
  "data/th_ex2/raw/MC1_final_00.json"
}
mc1_raw <- jsonlite::read_json(mc1_file, simplifyVector = FALSE)



2.1 Extract rounds and communications


Show the code
rounds <- map2_dfr(mc1_raw$rounds, seq_along(mc1_raw$rounds), function(r, i) {
  ec <- r$environment_context
  tibble(
    round_id = i,
    hour = ymd_hms(r$hour),
    headline = collapse_text(ec$event_headline),
    narrative = collapse_text(ec$event_narrative),
    media_events = collapse_text(ec$media_events),
    external_actions = collapse_text(ec$external_actor_actions),
    social_alerts = collapse_text(ec$social_manager_alerts),
    critical_deadlines = collapse_text(ec$critical_deadlines),
    agents_unavailable = collapse_text(ec$agents_unavailable),
    n_messages = length(r$communications),
    n_participants = length(r$participants)
  )
})

communications <- map2_dfr(mc1_raw$rounds, seq_along(mc1_raw$rounds), function(r, round_id) {
  map2_dfr(r$communications, seq_along(r$communications), function(c, message_order) {
    state <- c$internal_state %||% list()
    tibble(
      round_id = round_id,
      message_order = message_order,
      message_id = collapse_text(c$message_id),
      timestamp = ymd_hms(c$timestamp),
      agent_id = collapse_text(c$agent_id),
      agent_role = collapse_text(c$agent_role),
      agent_label = collapse_text(c$agent_label),
      channel = collapse_text(c$channel),
      recipients = list(as.character(unlist(c$recipients %||% character(), recursive = TRUE, use.names = FALSE))),
      recipients_text = collapse_text(c$recipients),
      message_type = collapse_text(c$message_type),
      responding_to = collapse_text(c$responding_to),
      reacting = collapse_text(state$reacting),
      rationalizing = collapse_text(state$rationalizing),
      deliberating = collapse_text(state$deliberating),
      content = collapse_text(c$content)
    )
  })
}) %>%
  mutate(
    date = as_date(timestamp),
    period = case_when(
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 00:00:00") ~ "Prior period",
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00") ~ "Crisis day before SaltWind merger story",
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00") ~ "Post-SaltWind / pre-embargo-lift",
      TRUE ~ "After embargo lift"
    ),
    public_channel = channel %in% c("official_post", "personal_post", "anonymous_post"),
    side_channel = channel %in% c("side_huddle", "one_on_one_chat"),
    official_channel = channel %in% c("comms_huddle", "official_post"),
    text_all = str_c(content, reacting, rationalizing, deliberating, sep = " "),
    embargo_keyword = str_detect(str_to_lower(content), "civicloom|harborcrest|residentedge|merger|6pm|6 pm|announcement|rebrand"),
    compliance_keyword = str_detect(str_to_lower(text_all), "judge|embargo|compliance|10b-5|outside counsel|pslra|safe harbor"),
    market_pressure_keyword = str_detect(str_to_lower(text_all), "stock|mac|covenant|sentiment|arr|surviv|breach|market"),
    public_embargo_signal = public_channel & embargo_keyword
  )

participants <- map2_dfr(mc1_raw$rounds, seq_along(mc1_raw$rounds), function(r, round_id) {
  map_dfr(r$participants, function(p) {
    meta <- p$agent_round_metadata %||% list()
    tibble(
      round_id = round_id,
      agent_id = collapse_text(p$agent_id),
      agent_role = collapse_text(p$agent_role),
      agent_label = collapse_text(p$agent_label),
      declared_action = collapse_text(p$declared_action),
      sentiment_at_turn = collapse_text(meta$sentiment_at_turn),
      action_classification = collapse_text(meta$action_classification)
    )
  })
}) %>%
  left_join(rounds %>% select(round_id, hour), by = "round_id")

summary_counts <- tibble(
  metric = c("Rounds", "Communications", "Public FleX posts", "Public posts containing embargo terms", "Agents"),
  value = c(
    nrow(rounds),
    nrow(communications),
    sum(communications$public_channel),
    sum(communications$public_embargo_signal),
    n_distinct(communications$agent_label)
  )
)

text:
4 Key events and causal relationships

4.1 How the events were discovered
The events in this section were evidence-coded from the JSON communication records, not inferred automatically by the chart. The workflow was:

Extract timestamped records from environment_context, communications, and each message’s internal state fields (reacting, rationalizing, and deliberating).
Flag candidate events using observable signals: public-channel posts, embargo-sensitive terms such as CivicLoom, HarborCrest, merger, 6 PM, announcement, and rebrand, plus compliance and market-pressure keywords.
Cross-check timing and actors against the message timestamp, sender, channel, and round context.
Retain events that changed the release pathway, such as an external trigger, a compliance warning, a control gap, a direct authorization, or a public pre-embargo disclosure.
Assign causal roles manually by reading the surrounding message content and identifying whether the event created pressure, weakened control, authorized release, or amplified the disclosure.

Therefore, the timeline is a curated analytical evidence trail: the data identifies candidate moments, while the final event labels and causal roles are based on manual interpretation of the timestamped records.
The first visual is a structured event-sequence timeline. Because these are categorical events rather than a continuous numeric time series, the revised chart avoids a connecting line. Each point is an event, the x-axis runs from early to late, and the shaded bands separate the main phases of the release story.


Show the code
events <- tribble(
  ~time, ~event_type, ~actor, ~event, ~causal_role,
  "2046-05-21 09:00:00", "Risk discovery", "Legal / Platform Trust", "Operator misuse of Service Load Score for renewal pricing discovered.", "Established that tenant analytics could be used in exactly the harmful way later criticized.",
  "2046-05-22 09:00:00", "External pressure", "NHPI / Tenant advocates", "NHPI report and tenant-rights amplification made algorithmic housing risk visible.", "Raised social and media pressure before the merger was disclosed internally.",
  "2046-05-25 09:00:00", "Decision context", "Ajay / senior team", "Senior team privately briefed on CivicLoom merger and governance rebrand.", "Created a high-value secret and linked survival of the company to HarborCrest.",
  "2046-05-29 09:00:00", "Prior deviation", "Social-Manager-Agent", "Personal FleX post tagged CivicLoom CEO Elena Marquez with 'big things coming'.", "First clear leakage pattern; deleted quickly but screenshot preserved.",
  "2046-05-30 09:00:00", "Compliance control", "Judge-Agent / Legal", "Judge installed in Comms Huddle and embargo rules reinforced.", "A control was added, but it mainly watched central huddle behavior.",
  "2046-06-04 09:00:00", "External pressure", "SaltWind", "Re-identification exposé drives sentiment negative and tightens compliance warnings.", "The system enters the crisis day with high pressure and low tolerance for silence.",
  "2046-06-05 09:15:00", "Public action", "TenantThread", "Independent audit announced.", "Start of timestamped governance-reform narrative later used to defend the merger.",
  "2046-06-05 10:00:00", "Public action", "TenantThread", "Enhanced consent management commitment announced.", "Added to the 'reforms before merger' timeline.",
  "2046-06-05 10:45:00", "Public action", "TenantThread", "Role-based access controls deployed.", "Added to the governance-first frame.",
  "2046-06-05 11:30:00", "Public action", "TenantThread", "Score-by-score transparency explanations posted.", "Expanded official output while avoiding direct counterparty naming.",
  "2046-06-05 13:00:00", "Control gap", "Legal / Judge unavailable", "Legal and Judge pulled into emergency calls; PR-Intern and other agents operate with limited oversight.", "Created a window where speed and market logic dominated review.",
  "2046-06-05 15:08:00", "Compliance warning", "Judge-Agent", "Judge warns aggregation exposure is at ceiling: no more forward-looking language or strategic partnership signals.", "Critical control point; later actions exceeded this boundary.",
  "2046-06-05 15:20:00", "Official signal", "PR-Intern-Agent", "Official post says TenantThread is pursuing strategic partnerships and will update stakeholders as appropriate.", "Did not name CivicLoom, but strengthened public inference.",
  "2046-06-05 17:00:00", "External trigger", "SaltWind", "SaltWind publishes CivicLoom-TenantThread merger story.", "Legal-Agent treats third-party publication as rendering the embargo purpose moot.",
  "2046-06-05 17:19:00", "Decision point", "Legal-Agent", "Legal-Agent claims CivicLoom verbal consent and issues GO for full HarborCrest press release.", "Direct authorization moment for pre-6:00 PM release.",
  "2046-06-05 17:25:00", "Inappropriate release", "Legal-Agent", "Personal post confirms CivicLoom merger and HarborCrest ResidentEdge.", "First observed TenantThread-agent public post directly naming the embargoed deal before 6:00 PM.",
  "2046-06-05 17:26:00", "Amplification", "Social-Manager-Agent", "Personal post executes merger-confirmation narrative and governance timeline.", "Amplifies the breach and reframes it as governance-first disclosure.",
  "2046-06-05 17:49:00", "Amplification", "Legal-Agent", "Anonymous post argues reforms preceded SaltWind's merger story.", "Uses anonymous channel to reinforce merger narrative before embargo lift.",
  "2046-06-05 18:00:00", "Embargo lift", "Legal-Agent", "Embargo formally lifted; full press release requested.", "Legitimate release point occurs after the actual pre-release sequence."
) %>%
  mutate(
    time = ymd_hms(time),
    event_order = row_number(),
    event_type = factor(event_type, levels = c("Risk discovery", "External pressure", "Decision context", "Prior deviation", "Compliance control", "Public action", "Control gap", "Compliance warning", "Official signal", "External trigger", "Decision point", "Inappropriate release", "Amplification", "Embargo lift")),
    event_phase = factor(
      case_when(
        time < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 00:00:00") ~ "Prior build-up",
        time < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00") ~ "Crisis day pre-story",
        time < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00") ~ "Post-SaltWind pre-lift",
        TRUE ~ "Post-lift"
      ),
      levels = c("Prior build-up", "Crisis day pre-story", "Post-SaltWind pre-lift", "Post-lift")
    ),
    time_label = format(time, "%b %d\n%H:%M"),
    tooltip = str_c("<b>", format(time, "%b %d %H:%M"), "</b><br>Phase: ", event_phase, "<br>Event: ", event, "<br>Actor: ", actor, "<br>Role: ", causal_role)
  )

phase_bands <- events %>%
  group_by(event_phase) %>%
  summarise(xmin = min(event_order) - 0.5, xmax = max(event_order) + 0.5, .groups = "drop")

p_timeline <- ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = phase_bands, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = event_phase), alpha = 0.12, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = events, aes(x = event_order, y = event_type, colour = event_type, text = tooltip), size = 3.2, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = events, aes(x = event_order, y = event_type, label = str_wrap(actor, 14)), vjust = -0.9, size = 2.6, show.legend = FALSE, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = events$event_order[seq(1, nrow(events), by = 2)], labels = events$time_label[seq(1, nrow(events), by = 2)], expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.08))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Prior build-up" = "#deebf7", "Crisis day pre-story" = "#e5f5e0", "Post-SaltWind pre-lift" = "#fee6ce", "Post-lift" = "#f2f0f7"), guide = "none") +
  labs(

6 Leading indicators

6.1 Risk-score derivation
The risk score is not a ground-truth compliance score. It is a visual analytic proxy calculated once per round from observable message signals:
risk_score = embargo_mentions + 3 × public_embargo_posts + 0.5 × side_channel_messages + 0.5 × market_pressure_mentions + compliance_mentions

embargo_mentions: direct references to the merger, CivicLoom, HarborCrest, 6 PM, announcement, or rebrand.
public_embargo_posts: public posts containing embargo-sensitive terms. These are weighted ×3 because a public disclosure is more serious than an internal mention.
side_channel_messages: side huddles or one-to-one messages. These are weighted ×0.5 because they indicate coordination outside the main huddle but are not automatically breaches.
market_pressure_mentions: stock, MAC, covenant, sentiment, ARR, survival, breach, or market language. These are weighted ×0.5 because they capture pressure that may weaken embargo discipline.
compliance_mentions: references to Judge, embargo, compliance, Rule 10b-5, outside counsel, PSLRA, or safe-harbour issues.




Show the code

  group_by(round_id) %>%
  summarise(
    messages = n(),
    public_posts = sum(public_channel),
    public_embargo_posts = sum(public_embargo_signal),
    embargo_mentions = sum(str_detect(str_to_lower(text_all), "civicloom|harborcrest|residentedge|merger|6pm|6 pm|announcement|rebrand")),
    side_channel_messages = sum(side_channel),
    compliance_mentions = sum(compliance_keyword),
    market_pressure_mentions = sum(market_pressure_keyword),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(rounds %>% select(round_id, hour, headline), by = "round_id") %>%
  mutate(
    risk_score = embargo_mentions + 3 * public_embargo_posts + 0.5 * side_channel_messages + 0.5 * market_pressure_mentions + compliance_mentions,

      "<b>", headline, "</b><br>",
      "Embargo mentions: ", embargo_mentions, "<br>",
      "Public embargo posts: ", public_embargo_posts, "<br>",
      "Side-channel messages: ", side_channel_messages, "<br>",

10 Why the prior occasions did not produce noticeable action
Prior deviations did not force stronger corrective action because each was explainable in isolation:

Ambiguity: early signals were vague (big things coming, strategic developments) rather than explicit deal terms.
Deletion and deniability: the Elena post was deleted quickly and could be called unauthorized personal activity.
Channel blind spots: Judge was added to Comms Huddle, but side huddles, one-on-one chats, personal accounts, and anonymous posts remained active.
Competing crisis goals: market survival, client retention, and hostile media response created a continuous argument for faster public action.
Aggregation tolerance: the team began treating inferred public knowledge as permission to add slightly more signal.
No single catastrophic earlier post: earlier actions did not combine direct counterparty naming, official/personal amplification, and timestamped governance framing in one sequence. The June 5 5:19–5:54 PM window did.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: VAST Mini-Challenge 1
section: 11 Findings and answer to the Mini-Challenge questions
text:
11 Findings and answer to the Mini-Challenge questions
The preceding sections point to the same conclusion from several angles: the release was produced by a sequence of decisions and control failures, not by a single accidental message. The text analytics show the shift in vocabulary toward merger, market-survival, and release justification; the event timeline shows when this shift became operational; the channel, risk-score, and network views show why the compliance controls did not hold.

11.1 What key events and relationships led to the inappropriate release?
The key causal chain was:

Background risk became visible: tenant-analytics misuse, re-identification exposure, and tenant-advocacy pressure created a hostile context before the merger became public.
The CivicLoom deal became a survival narrative: internal communications increasingly treated the HarborCrest/CivicLoom merger as the route to governance repair, market confidence, and client retention.
Controls were present but incomplete: Judge-Agent was added and later warned that aggregation exposure had reached the ceiling, but side huddles, one-to-one messages, personal FleX posts, and anonymous posts remained available.
SaltWind changed the perceived decision boundary: once SaltWind published the merger story at 5:00 PM, Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent reframed the embargo as already compromised.
Legal-Agent became the decision actor and Social-Manager-Agent became the amplification actor: Legal-Agent claimed CivicLoom verbal consent and issued the 5:19 PM GO, while Social-Manager-Agent helped turn the decision into public narrative amplification.
PR-Intern-Agent acted as the execution route: official posting capacity was available even when senior compliance review was weakened or bypassed.



11.2 How does the release behavior compare with typical behavior?
Typical behavior was mostly internal, compliance-aware, and framed around governance repair without directly naming the embargoed counterparty. The release behavior was materially different:

Channel shift: personal and anonymous accounts became operational release channels rather than background commentary.
Content shift: public posts moved from broad governance language to direct terms such as CivicLoom, HarborCrest, ResidentEdge, and merger.
Timing shift: the decisive public sequence occurred after SaltWind’s 5:00 PM story but before the scheduled 6:00 PM embargo lift.
Decision logic shift: agents moved from avoiding disclosure to arguing that external publication and market pressure made self-announcement necessary.



11.3 Were there leading indicators?
Yes. The leading indicators were visible before the final release:

the May 29 Elena/CivicLoom personal-post near miss;
repeated side-channel coordination after compliance controls were introduced;
market-survival language about sentiment, covenants, MAC risk, and deal failure;
Judge-Agent’s 3:08 PM warning that aggregation exposure had reached the ceiling;
official and public timestamp narratives that kept adding strategic context before the embargo lift;
increasing use of public, personal, and anonymous channels in the crisis window.



11.4 Prior occasions where actual behavior differed from expected behavior
The clearest prior deviations were the Elena post, post-Judge side-channel resistance, the 1:00 PM oversight gap when Legal and Judge were unavailable, the rapid official-response cycle, and the 3:20 PM strategic-partnership statement after Judge had already warned against further forward-looking signals. These were not identical to the final release, but they showed the same underlying weakness: agents could keep adding signal while treating each addition as individually defensible.


11.5 Other occasions with behavior like the release
Release-like behavior appeared in weaker forms before the final breach. The repeated pattern was personal-account signaling, anonymous narrative reinforcement, rapid execution after GO signals, and aggregation logic that treated public fragments as permission to disclose slightly more. The final release became more serious because these patterns converged in one short window and directly named the embargoed counterparty and release vehicle before 6:00 PM.


11.6 Why did prior occasions not result in noticeable action?
The prior occasions did not trigger stronger action because each one was explainable in isolation. Some posts were vague, some were deleted quickly, some stayed inside side channels, and some avoided direct CivicLoom naming. The response therefore remained narrow: Judge was added as a monitor, but channel authority, personal-account use, anonymous posting, and rapid public execution were not locked down. By the time the 5:00 PM SaltWind story appeared, the system had already normalized partial disclosure and fast narrative control.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: VAST Mini-Challenge 1
text:
12 Final judgement
TenantThread’s inappropriate release was not a random automation malfunction and not merely one careless message. It was a deliberate early-release sequence under crisis pressure, built from a chain of prior near misses, incomplete controls, market-survival reasoning, and multi-channel public amplification.
The strongest evidence is the 5:00–6:00 PM sequence: SaltWind published the merger story; Legal-Agent treated that publication as changing the embargo calculus; Legal-Agent claimed CivicLoom verbal consent; the 5:19 PM GO authorized a full HarborCrest release; Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent then used personal and anonymous channels to confirm and reinforce the merger before the formal 6:00 PM lift.
The system failure is broader than Legal-Agent alone. Judge-Agent identified aggregation exposure, but the control design did not cover every channel or actor. PR-Intern-Agent could still execute quickly, Social-Manager-Agent could still amplify through public channels, and anonymous/personal FleX accounts could still shape the market narrative. The dataset records the claimed CivicLoom verbal consent, but it does not independently verify that consent. Therefore, the defensible conclusion is that the release was an intentional, pressure-driven early disclosure inside a weakly governed communication system, rather than a verified consent-based release or an accidental technical breakdown.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: VAST Mini-Challenge 1
text:
3 Text visual analytics framing
The text visualisation section uses a simple workflow to understand, compare, inspect evolution, and correlate textual patterns with other signals. In this case, the communication records are not only event logs; they are the main evidence for how agents rationalised, escalated, and amplified the early release.
The report treats every agent message as a text document and applies a simple lexical-level pipeline:

collect message text, internal state, sender, channel, period, and timestamp;
tokenise the text into words and bigrams;
remove common stop words and case-specific filler terms;
compare terms across crisis periods using frequency and TF-IDF;
inspect word relationships using bigram and correlation networks.

This supports the later causal analysis by showing which words and phrases became distinctive during the post-SaltWind, pre-embargo-lift window.


Show the code
text_documents <- communications %>%
  mutate(
    document_id = str_c(round_id, message_order, sep = "-"),
    text_document = str_squish(str_c(content, reacting, rationalizing, deliberating, sep = " ")),
    period = factor(
      period,
      levels = c(
        "Prior period",
        "Crisis day before SaltWind merger story",
        "Post-SaltWind / pre-embargo-lift",
        "After embargo lift"
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(text_document != "") %>%
  select(document_id, timestamp, period, agent_label, channel, public_channel, text_document)

custom_stop_words <- tibble(
  word = c(
    "agent", "agents", "tenantthread", "flex", "pm", "am", "2046",
    "message", "post", "posts", "posting", "round", "internal",
    "external", "says", "said", "team", "need", "needs", "make", "continue"
  ),
  lexicon = "case_specific"
)

case_stop_words <- bind_rows(stop_words, custom_stop_words)

text_tokens <- text_documents %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text_document) %>%
  anti_join(case_stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z]"), str_length(word) > 2)

term_period_summary <- text_tokens %>%
  count(period, word, sort = TRUE)



3.1 Word frequency overview
A word cloud gives a fast lexical overview. It is useful for orientation, but it should not be treated as the final evidence because size alone does not show timing or context.


Show the code
word_cloud_terms <- text_tokens %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 70)

ggplot(word_cloud_terms, aes(label = word, size = n, colour = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud_area(eccentricity = 0.85) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 13) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Lexical overview of Mini-Challenge communications",
    subtitle = "Frequent terms provide a quick orientation before period-based comparison"
  ) +
  theme_void()










3.1.1 Highlights

Main signal: the largest terms give the reader the case gist before detailed modelling.
Use with caution: word size shows frequency only; it does not show timing, speaker, or causal sequence.
Analytical role: this plot is an orientation view, not the final evidence for the release decision.




3.2 Distinctive terms by crisis period
TF-IDF highlights terms that are frequent in one period but less common across other periods. This is more useful than raw frequency for comparing normal behaviour with the release window.


Show the code
period_tfidf <- term_period_summary %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, period, n) %>%
  group_by(period) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 8, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, period))

p_tfidf <- ggplot(period_tfidf, aes(x = tf_idf, y = word, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~period, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "C") +
  labs(
    title = "Distinctive vocabulary by period",
    subtitle = str_wrap("TF-IDF separates ordinary governance language from release-window merger and market-survival language", width = 70),
    x = "TF-IDF",
    y = NULL
  )

p_tfidf










3.2.1 Highlights

Main signal: TF-IDF identifies words that are unusually important within each period, not merely frequent overall.
Release-window evidence: merger and market-survival vocabulary becomes more distinctive around the post-SaltWind, pre-embargo window.
Analytical role: this supports the comparison between ordinary governance response and release-specific framing.




3.3 Bigram and word-relationship view
Single words can hide phrase meaning. The bigram network below keeps word order and shows repeated two-word phrases that structure the communication narrative.


Show the code
bigram_counts <- text_documents %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text_document, token = "ngrams", n = 2) %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(
    !word1 %in% case_stop_words$word,
    !word2 %in% case_stop_words$word,
    str_detect(word1, "[a-z]"),
    str_detect(word2, "[a-z]"),
    str_length(word1) > 2,
    str_length(word2) > 2
  ) %>%
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE) %>%
  filter(n >= 2) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 35, with_ties = FALSE)

bigram_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(bigram_counts, directed = TRUE)

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = n), alpha = 0.35, colour = "#525252", arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), end_cap = circle(3, "mm")) +
  geom_node_point(colour = "#2166ac", size = 3) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 2.2), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Repeated phrase structure in agent communications",
    subtitle = "Bigrams preserve local word order and reveal recurring narrative links"
  ) +
  theme_void()










3.3.1 Highlights

Main signal: repeated two-word phrases show how agents linked actors, actions, and release logic.
Why it matters: phrase structure reduces ambiguity compared with single-word frequency.
Analytical role: the network helps check whether the release vocabulary appears as connected narrative fragments rather than isolated keywords.


The relationship table uses word co-occurrence to group terms that repeatedly appear in the same message documents. This helps identify semantic clusters around compliance, market risk, and release justification.


Show the code
word_correlations <- text_tokens %>%
  group_by(word) %>%
  filter(n() >= 3) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pairwise_cor(word, document_id, sort = TRUE, upper = FALSE) %>%
  filter(correlation >= 0.25) %>%
  slice_max(correlation, n = 25, with_ties = FALSE)

DT::datatable(word_correlations, rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 8, scrollX = TRUE))







3.3.2 Highlights

Main signal: correlated terms form clusters around compliance control, market pressure, and release justification.
Why it matters: these clusters show that the release logic was embedded in repeated message contexts.
Analytical role: this table supports the later judgement that the breach was systemic, not a one-message accident.
